items.prompt: Where does the Rafflesia arnoldii plant get its nutrients?

options.label: From its own roots and leaves
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Rafflesia arnoldii has no roots, stems, or leaves; it does not make its own food.

options.label: From the air and sunlight
options.feedback: This is incorrect because without chlorophyll, Rafflesia cannot photosynthesize, so it cannot use sunlight to make food.

options.label: From the roots and stems of a host vine
options.feedback: Correct. Rafflesia is parasitic and attaches to the roots and stems of wild East Indian grape vines to draw nutrients from them.

options.label: From the soil around it
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Rafflesia has no roots of its own to absorb water and minerals from the soil.

items.ok_line: Rafflesia lives on a host vine.
items.exp_text: Rafflesia arnoldii is parasitic, so it takes water and nutrients directly from the roots and stems of its host vine. Because it lacks roots, stems, leaves, and chlorophyll, it cannot make its own food or absorb from the soil.

items.prompt: What is the pelican flower's most notable feature?

options.label: It has the largest flower in the world
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the largest flower belongs to Rafflesia arnoldii; the pelican flower instead holds the record for the longest flower.

options.label: Its single sepal can be up to 3 or 4 metres long
options.feedback: Correct. The pelican flower's one sepal extends to a remarkable length, making it the longest flower and the largest single sepal.

options.label: It is the smallest complete flower
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the smallest complete flower is Parish's wild buckwheat, not the pelican flower.

options.label: It produces millions of tiny florets
options.feedback: This is incorrect because that describes Balanophora involucrata's inflorescence, not the pelican flower.

items.ko_line: Its record is length, not size.
items.exp_text: The pelican flower (Aristolochia grandiflora) holds the record for the world's longest flower. Its greatly expanded calyx develops into a single sepal that can stretch up to 3 metres, or possibly 4 metres, in length, which is also the largest single sepal known.

items.prompt: What does Balanophora involucrata produce on its capitate inflorescence?

options.label: Millions of tiny flowers
options.feedback: Correct. Its round, head-like inflorescence contains as many as ten million tiny florets, each only 25 micrometres wide.

options.label: One very large flower
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Balanophora produces many tiny flowers, not a single large one.

options.label: A single sepal that grows very long
options.feedback: This is incorrect because that is a feature of the pelican flower, not Balanophora involucrata.

options.label: Fruits that are the smallest in the world
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the smallest fruits belong to the Wolffia genus, not to Balanophora.

items.ok_line: Millions of florets on one head.
items.ko_line: Balanophora's head is made of many.
items.exp_text: Balanophora involucrata, found in the Himalayas, has a capitate (head-shaped) inflorescence that holds an enormous number of miniature flowers. Each floret is just 25 micrometres wide, and a single capitulum may contain up to ten million of them.

items.prompt: What makes Parish's wild buckwheat the smallest complete flower?

options.label: It has no petals
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Parish's wild buckwheat has all four basic organs, including petals — it has 3 petals.

options.label: It is a single tiny floret without sepals
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it has 3 sepals as part of its complete structure.

options.label: It has only stamens and carpels
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a complete flower must have sepals and petals too, and this one does.

options.label: It has all four basic organs but is only 0.6 mm long
options.feedback: Correct. Despite having sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels, the whole flower is merely 0.6 mm long.

items.ko_line: It has every part it needs.
items.exp_text: Parish's wild buckwheat (Eriogonum parishii) is the smallest complete flower because it possesses all four basic organs — 3 sepals, 3 petals, 3 stamens, and a pistil of 3 carpels — yet the entire flower measures only 0.6 mm in length.

items.prompt: Which plant has the largest branched inflorescence?

options.label: Titan arum
options.feedback: This is incorrect because titan arum has the largest unbranched inflorescence, not a branched one.

options.label: Pelican flower
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the pelican flower is a single flower, not an inflorescence, and it is not branched.

options.label: Talipot palm
options.feedback: Correct. The talipot palm (Corypha umbraculifera) produces the largest branched inflorescence in the plant world.

options.label: Rafflesia arnoldii
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Rafflesia is a single huge flower, not a branched inflorescence.

items.exp_text: The talipot palm (Corypha umbraculifera) has the largest branched inflorescence of any plant. It lives for up to 60 years and flowers only once in its lifetime, producing that enormous branched cluster of flowers.

items.prompt: What is the titan arum best known for?

options.label: Having the largest flower in the world
options.feedback: This is incorrect because its claim is about the inflorescence, not a single flower; Rafflesia holds the largest flower record.

options.label: Having the largest unbranched inflorescence
options.feedback: Correct. The titan arum produces the biggest unbranched inflorescence, and it is also known as the corpse flower.

options.label: Having the longest sepal of any plant
options.feedback: This is incorrect because that record belongs to the pelican flower.

options.label: Producing the smallest fruit in the world
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the smallest fruit belongs to Wolffia, not to the titan arum.

items.exp_text: The titan arum (Amorphophallus titanum) has the largest unbranched inflorescence in the world. It is called the corpse flower because of the carrion-like smell it produces; its inflorescence is not as large as the talipot palm's, but that palm's is branched.

items.prompt: What is the current heaviest fruit on record?

options.label: A pumpkin
options.feedback: Correct. The heaviest fruit ever recorded is a pumpkin weighing about 1.247 tonnes, grown in California in 2023.

options.label: A jackfruit
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the record is specifically for a pumpkin, not a jackfruit.

options.label: A watermelon
options.feedback: This is incorrect because no watermelon holds the record; a pumpkin does.

options.label: A cacao pod
options.feedback: This is incorrect because cacao pods are not the heaviest; the heaviest is a pumpkin.

items.exp_text: The heaviest fruit known is a pumpkin that weighed 1.247 tonnes, grown in California in 2023. No other fruit has matched that weight, so it stands as the world record.

items.prompt: Which plant has the smallest fruit in the world?

options.label: Balanophora involucrata
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Balanophora is known for its tiny flowers, not for its fruit.

options.label: Parish's wild buckwheat
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Parish's wild buckwheat is noted for its tiny complete flower, not for the smallest fruit.

options.label: Pelican flower
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the pelican flower is known for its long sepal, not for small fruits.

options.label: Wolffia
options.feedback: Correct. Species in the Wolffia genus, such as Wolffia angusta and Wolffia globosa, produce the smallest and lightest fruits in the world.

items.ko_line: This is about fruit, not flowers.
items.exp_text: Plants in the genus Wolffia have the smallest and lightest fruits known. For example, Wolffia angusta's fruit is only 0.30 mm long and weighs about 70 micrograms, yet it is one of the largest fruits relative to the parent plant's size.

items.prompt: What is unusual about the fruit of Wolffia compared to the size of its parent plant?

options.label: It is much larger than the whole plant
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the fruit is smaller than the plant; the plant is less than a millimetre long, and the fruit is about a third of that.

options.label: It is the same size as the plant
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the fruit is only a fraction of the plant's length, not equal.

options.label: It is large relative to the parent plant
options.feedback: Correct. Although the fruit is tiny in absolute size, it takes up a third or more of the parent plant's length, making it proportionally large.

options.label: It is smaller than the plant's flowers
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the fruit is relatively large compared to the plant, and the plant's size is about a millimetre or less.

items.ok_line: Fruit is a third of the plant.
items.ko_line: But the plant is tiny too.
items.exp_text: Wolffia plants are less than a millimetre long, and their fruit is about 0.30 mm long. This means the fruit is relatively large for the plant, taking up a third or more of the parent plant's length, even though it is the smallest fruit in the world.

items.prompt: Which plant is known as the 'corpse flower'?

options.label: Rafflesia arnoldii only
options.feedback: This is incorrect because while Rafflesia is sometimes called by that name, the more well-known one is the titan arum.

options.label: Titan arum
options.feedback: Correct. The titan arum (Amorphophallus titanum) is commonly called the corpse flower because of its carrion-like smell.

options.label: Pelican flower
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the pelican flower is not called the corpse flower; it is known for its long sepal.

options.label: Talipot palm
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the talipot palm is known for its branched inflorescence, not as a corpse flower.

items.ko_line: Rafflesia is only sometimes named so.
items.exp_text: The titan arum is widely known as the corpse flower because it produces a fleshy smell resembling a rotting corpse. The name is also sometimes applied to Rafflesia, but the titan arum is the primary holder of this common name.
